October 2036. Elena has written her first practice forum text. Katrin Krüger, the journalist, corrects it in the café.
Elena, your text is lovely. Really. But it won't get full marks like this.
Why not? I wrote two hundred and twenty words. More than required.
That's not the problem. The task has four points. You covered three points at great length and forgot the fourth. That costs a lot.
“Name other possibilities.” You only wrote about the care home. But there's also home care, multi-generational houses, assisted living.
I thought a good story was better than four points.
At a newspaper, yes. In an exam, no. First the four points. Then, if there's room, the story. And one more thing: you write “man” twelve times.
Not wrong. Boring. Vary it: passive, “viele Menschen”, “ältere Menschen”, “wer …”. That shows the examiners you're speaking at B2 level.
And the second task? The formal email?
That one was good. Except for the ending. You don't write “Liebe Grüße” to the manager of a care home. “Mit freundlichen Grüßen.” Always.

For writing, Elena had the best teacher to be found on Kastanienallee, and the strictest. Katrin Krüger had written for Berlin newspapers for thirty years, reports, portraits, commentaries, and in those thirty years, as she put it, she had “torn up more trainees' texts than Hotte had checked tickets”. She came to the café every evening at six, after the newsroom, sat down at the table by the window, ordered a black coffee and took out of her handbag the red pen, the same one with which she had corrected Ludwig's proofs a year before. Then Elena put the text of the day in front of her, and Katrin read it twice without saying a word, and then started writing, and Elena watched the page slowly turn red.

The first topic for the forum post, which Elif had picked from the model test without much thought, was one that touched Elena at once: “Should elderly people who need help live in a care home or at home with their family?” There were four points to cover: your own opinion, reasons, experiences from your own country, other possibilities. Elena wrote for an hour without looking up. She wrote about her own grandmother from a village near Sibiu, who until her death had lived under the same roof as her daughter, Elena's mother, and about the warmth of that house, and about her mother's exhaustion in the last years, which nobody had talked about. She wrote about Grete, who wasn't alone in the care home but surrounded by people, by music, by children who came every Wednesday. It was, as Katrin said later, a very good text. And it wouldn't have passed.

“You've forgotten the fourth point”, said Katrin, pointing with the red pen at the task. “Other possibilities. Home care with a care service. Multi-generational houses. Assisted living. Shared flats for older people. Those are four possibilities and you haven't named any of them.” Elena wanted to protest, but Katrin raised her hand. “In an exam”, she said, “the task is like a tram timetable. You have to stop at every stop. Even at the ones that seem boring to you. If you skip a stop, it doesn't matter how beautifully you drove between the others.” Ludwig, who was sitting at the next table pretending to read the newspaper, nodded vigorously. “Exactly”, he said. “In nineteen seventy I once skipped the Kollwitzplatz stop. By mistake. It cost me a week's wages.”

Then came the problem with “man”. Katrin had circled every “man” in the text in red, and there were twelve, and on the page it looked, as Elif remarked, “as if the text had measles”. “Man muss bedenken”, “man kann sagen”, “man sollte”, “wenn man alt ist”. Katrin explained that “man” isn't wrong, but that the examiners want to see whether someone can handle different structures. “Instead of «man muss bedenken» write «Es sollte bedacht werden». Instead of «wenn man alt ist» write «wer älter wird» or «im Alter». Instead of «man kann sagen»: «Es lässt sich sagen». It's the same thing, but it shows you've learned the chapters on the passive and the alternatives to the passive.” Elena wrote each variant in her twelfth notebook, on a new page, under the heading: “Against the measles.”

The next evening Elena brought a new version. She hadn't made the text longer, but shorter, a hundred and seventy words, and had put each of the four points in a separate paragraph, with a clear first sentence, as Katrin had shown her. Her grandmother's story was still there, but only in three sentences, as an example for the point “experiences from your own country”. And Grete was still there, in a single sentence in the conclusion: “I know a woman who at a hundred lives in a care home and is less lonely there than many people in their own flats.” Katrin read the text twice. Then she circled nothing. She just wrote at the bottom of the page, in red: “All stops served. On time. Full marks.” Elena read it and laughed, and Ludwig at the next table said, without looking up from his newspaper: “See? Kollwitzplatz.”

The second task, the formal message, was different from the start. For the first practice test Elif hadn't taken a task from the model test but had invented one herself, and when Elena read it, she understood why. “You would like a resident of the care home, who is very ill, to be able to receive a visit every day from a young pianist, including outside visiting hours. Write to the care home management. Explain the situation, ask for an exception, propose a solution.” Elena looked at Elif. Elif was looking at the table. “It isn't an exercise”, said Elif quietly. “Mrs Petersen says she's not allowed to decide on her own. It has to be requested in writing. And Mum doesn't write German well enough. And I'm twelve. Nobody takes me seriously.”

Hotte, who of course was listening too, because it happened to be Thursday, shook his head. “Formal letters”, he said scornfully. “In the GDR I wrote twenty-two formal letters, for a flat with a bathroom. Every one began with «Dear comrades». Every one ended with «With socialist greetings». I got the bathroom in nineteen eighty-nine. In October. Three weeks later the Wall was gone, and nobody cared about my bathroom any more.” He looked at Elena, more seriously than usual. “But if you write the letter”, he said, “then write it properly. With everything. Subject, greeting, request, solution. Mrs Petersen is an official with a heart. But the official first. Then the heart. You have to convince the official first. The heart then comes by itself.”

Grete had been worse for three weeks. She barely ate any more, slept most of the time, and when she was awake she asked for music. Elif came every Wednesday, as she had for three years, but Wednesday was only once a week, and visiting hours ended at six p.m., and Elif had school until half past three and piano lessons and homework. When she came on other days, at six or half past six, she had to leave again. The rules were for everyone, Mrs Petersen said, genuinely sorry, and she couldn't make an exception without a written request, which she had to pass on to the supervisory authority. That was what the regulations said. And so that evening Elena sat in the café, with the task Elif had invented, which wasn't invented, and wrote the most important letter she had ever written in German.

She wrote slowly. She thought about every point on the list. Subject: “Request for an exception regarding visits to Mrs Margarete Hoffmann, room 14.” Greeting: “Dear Mrs Petersen,” and then, with a small letter: “I am writing to you with a request.” She explained who Elif was, how long she had been visiting Mrs Hoffmann, how important music was for the resident, “according to her doctor and her family”. She asked for an exception: that Elif might stay until eight p.m. on every day she could manage, “for thirty minutes at most, quietly, with consideration for the other residents”. And she proposed a solution she was proud of herself: during this time Elif could play the old grand piano in the common room, with the door open, so that other residents who couldn't sleep in the evening could listen too.

Katrin read the letter once. Then a second time. Then she put down the red pen without having underlined anything, which, as Ludwig claimed later, had never happened in thirty years. She corrected only one thing, right at the end, in pencil, not in red: out of habit Elena had written “Liebe Grüße”. Katrin crossed it out and wrote above it: “Mit freundlichen Grüßen”. Then she looked at Elena. “It's the best formal letter I've read this year”, she said. “Including the letters from my newsroom.” She hesitated. “But «Liebe Grüße» would have cost you almost a point. And Mrs Petersen is a woman who cares about such things.”

Elena copied the letter out once more, by hand, on good paper that Lena had brought her from the stationer's on the corner, and signed it. Then she gave it to Elif to sign too, and Elif signed with her full name, Elif Yilmaz, in her round, neat handwriting, and underneath, after a brief hesitation, she added: “Author of the book «Das Mädchen am Tisch», Winter Verlag, second edition.” Elena laughed. “That doesn't belong in a formal letter”, she said. Elif shrugged. “Katrin said you have to give reasons why you should be taken seriously”, she said. “That's my reason.” Katrin, who had been listening, nodded. “Leave it”, she said. “It's an argument.”

The answer came two days later, by post, on the care home's letterhead, in perfect bureaucratic German, which by now Elena could read without asking Ludwig. “Dear Mrs Ionescu, dear Miss Yilmaz, following the examination of your request by the care home management, in consultation with the attending physician, your request is hereby granted.” Below came conditions: thirty minutes at most, consideration for the night-time quiet, informing the care staff. And right at the end, under Mrs Petersen's signature, there was, handwritten, in small, neat writing, a postscript that didn't belong in a formal letter: “The piano in the common room was tuned yesterday. I paid for it myself. Mrs Hoffmann donated it to the home in 1998. It was time. S. P.”

That evening Elif played for the first time outside visiting hours, at a quarter past seven, in the common room, on the freshly tuned piano, with the door open. She played the little Chopin waltz she had practised on the kitchen table, and then the Brahms Intermezzo. Grete lay in her room, two doors along, with her eyes closed. Mara, who was on duty on another ward that evening but had come over in her break, sat by Grete's bed holding her hand. At the first notes Grete didn't open her eyes. But her fingers moved on the blanket, very slightly, as if they were playing too, on a table only she could see. And from the other rooms, one after another, the doors quietly opened. Elena stood in the corridor and listened. She had, she thought, taken many exams in her life. But none that had brought so many points.

When Elif had finished and went quietly into Grete's room to say good night, Grete was awake. She looked at Elif, for a long time, with her clear gaze, which had clouded over in the last weeks but that evening was as clear as it used to be. “The piano”, she whispered. “It's tuned.” Elif nodded. “Mrs Petersen had it tuned”, she said. “Because of the letter.” Grete smiled. “In nineteen ninety-eight”, she whispered, “I brought it here. I said it should be played. By children. It waited thirty-eight years.” She closed her eyes. “Now it has its child.” Elif sat on the edge of the bed and stayed until Mara told her it was time. On the way home she didn't say a word. But at home she wrote in her diary, for the first time in German and not in Turkish: “Today I learned that a letter can make music.” Underneath, smaller: “Yours sincerely. Not lots of love.”
